newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nuclear deadlock threatens Swedish gov't alliance.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear deadlock threatens Swedish gov't alliance.

text.p: A row over when to shut down Sweden's nuclear industry is threatening the country's governing alliance, with the small Centre Party on Thursday refusing to accept a delay until the next century.

The ruling Social Democrats had promised to close the first of Sweden's 12 nuclear reactors by the autumn of 1998 but in recent weeks the Energy Minister Anders Sundstrom has said this timing was no longer feasible.
The government's informal coalition partner and closest ally, the Centre Party, is pressuring the government to stick to the agreed timetable.
"We believe that they will stick to their platform," Lennart Daleus, the Centre Party's energy negotiator, told Reuters.
"We are convinced that one reactor will be closed before general elections in 1998."

If the Centre Party withdrew its support from the minority government, some of the other five parties in parliament could take its place or the government could rely on support from different parties on different issues.
Sundstrom is under pressure from electricity-intensive industries to allow the reactors to operate until they are too old, which would be around the year 2020 or 2025.
Sundstrom said he now expected the first reactor to be closed in 2001. "A decision about closing one reactor will be taken before elections in 1998," Sundstrom told Reuters.

If the government follows Sundstrom's line, the disagreement could end the close ties between the minority government, which holds about 46 percent of Sweden's 349 parliamentary seats, and the Centre Party, that has nearly eight percent.
The nuclear issue is an important part of the Centre Party manifesto, with the party seeking a total ban on nuclear power. It has previously left coalitions rather than compromise.
Daleus declined to say if the Centre Party would turn its back on Prime Minister Goran Persson's government if the Social Democrats did not go through with the promised closure.

The nuclear shut-down was mooted in the early 1980s when Swedes voted in a national referendum to gradually phase out nuclear power and the parliament set 2010 as the target for making Sweden nuclear-free.
Nuclear power meets about half of the country's electricity needs, the rest being generated by hydro-electric power.
But the government has promised not to dam any more rivers, so an increase in hydro-electric power can be excluded.
The same goes for natural gas as parliament in 1993 ruled that in the year 2000, carbon dioxide emissions should not exceed 1990 levels and should decline after the year 2000.
Electricity intensive industries have stressed that no other electricity is as cheap as nuclear and hydro-electric power and they fear higher electricity prices.
